name: Rosalind "Roz" Vance

inspiration.oldScript: Carrie and Prom Night made the outcast girl's body and sexuality monstrous, and in the genre the queer girl dies.
inspiration.newLens: Two girls whose love was erased by a cruel prank. Roz's menace is grief at the town that wrote her out, and her Best ending is a last dance: release, not revenge.

logline: Every couple in Glimmer Falls is dreaming of the same 1966 prom, and the girl in the rain-soaked crown will not let anyone leave the floor until she gets her dance.
backstory: In May 1966 Rosalind "Roz" Vance was voted Spring Queen of Glimmer Falls High: track star, terrible singer, the kind of girl who laughed with her whole face. She was also secretly in love with Delphine Hart, the quiet senior who rode a secondhand motorcycle and read poetry in the bleachers. They had a plan. When the band struck up the queen's dance, Roz would walk past the Spring King and ask Delphine instead, in front of everyone. Three boys found the letter Roz wrote about it. They forged a note in Delphine's handwriting, Meet me on the gym roof before the crowning, look at the stars, and when Roz climbed up they took the ladder away so she would miss her big moment. Then the spring storm came. Roz tried to climb down the drainpipe in her gown. The school called it a terrible accident involving a silly girl who went where she should not. The boys were never named. The yearbook printed her photo beside the Spring King, and Delphine was not allowed at the funeral. Twenty years later the Heartstone has woken Roz in her crown of wilted gardenias, still waiting for the dance the whole town pretended was never going to happen.

centralIssue.title: Love that was erased
centralIssue.summary: Roz did not die because she loved a girl. She died because three boys thought that love was a joke, and then the whole town buried the truth with her. Her rage is real, but it is grief with nowhere to go. Uncover what the yearbook hid, who took the ladder and what song she meant to dance to, and give Roz and Delphine the last dance they were promised.

poster: A teenage girl ghost in a rain-soaked mint 1966 prom gown and a crown of wilted gardenias standing on the roof of a high school gym in a lightning storm, below her a suburban street of couples slow-dancing in their pajamas, paper moons drifting up into the clouds
portrait: Close portrait of a 1960s prom queen ghost, dark curls plastered by rain, freckles, a crooked tiara woven with brown-edged gardenias, mascara streaked, a fierce and heartbroken smile, lit pale green by a gym exit sign
endingPhoto: A teenage girl ghost in a rain-soaked mint 1966 prom gown and a crown of wilted gardenias floating above a high school gym stage in a lightning storm, a single spotlight on her, crepe paper streamers whipping around, a crowd of teens in rented tuxedos and puffy dresses frozen mid-slow-dance on the gym floor below
taunts: Hold on tight. They'll tell you it never happened.
Twenty years I've been waiting by the punch bowl. You can wait one song.
They called it an accident. Do I look like an accident?

clues.title: The photo they never printed
clues.hint: The yearbook office at Glimmer Falls High keeps every negative since the school opened, even the ones somebody said not to print.

encounter.title: Do Not Print
encounter.text: The yearbook office smells like fixer and old pizza. The 1966 Glimmer Light yearbook is open on the light table to a memorial page: Roz Vance in her crown, smiling beside a square-jawed boy, captioned Our Queen and Her King, Forever. Behind you, a gray filing drawer labeled DEAD FILES 1966 slides open by itself, just an inch, the way a door opens when someone wants you to follow.
encounter.art: A cluttered high school yearbook office, an old 1966 school annual lying open on a glowing light table to a page with a black-and-white photo of a smiling prom queen beside a square-jawed boy, a gray steel filing drawer behind it sliding open an inch by itself, a single wet footprint on the linoleum, a teenager turning toward the drawer, white light-table glow and a dim desk lamp, medium shot

choices.label: Hold every 1966 negative up to the light table

success.text: Strip forty-one, frame six: two girls in the bleachers sharing one milkshake with two straws, laughing so hard they are blurry. The sleeve is stamped DO NOT PRINT, PER PRINCIPAL. On the back, in looping pen: R + D, Spring '66. The girl with the straw is Roz. The other one, you realize slowly, is Ms. Hart from the library.
success.art: A film negative held up to a glowing light table showing two 1960s teenage girls laughing in gym bleachers sharing a milkshake, a sleeve with a red restricted stamp beside it

failure.text: The negatives slide out of your hands like wet leaves. Every frame you pick up shows the same thing: an empty gym roof in the rain. When you look at the memorial page again, the Spring King's face has been scratched out, and the caption now reads, in dripping ink, NOT HIM.
failure.art: Scattered film negatives on a yearbook office floor all showing an empty gym roof in rain, a yearbook page with a boy's face scratched out and a fresh angry ink scrawl

choices.label: Ask the yearbook editor what the dead files are for

success.text: Wendy Ostrowski, senior editor and permanent resident of this room, pushes up her glasses. "Stuff the principal killed. Smoking, protest signs, two boys holding hands at the '71 picnic." She digs out a 1966 sleeve without looking. "This one gets me. They printed her with the king. Look who she actually wanted to be photographed with."
success.art: A bespectacled teen yearbook editor in a cardigan covered in buttons handing a negative sleeve to another teenager across a cluttered desk, a hobby knife and rubber cement nearby

failure.text: Wendy is on deadline and throws you out with the words "I have forty senior quotes to censor." On the way out the trophy case fogs over from inside, and a finger writes on the glass in neat cursive: ask about the roof.
failure.art: A high school trophy case fogging over from the inside, a ghostly finger writing in cursive on the glass, a dusty 1966 spring queen tiara on the top shelf

clues.title: The man who took the ladder
clues.hint: The owner of Pump Iron Gym went to Glimmer Falls High in 1966. He lifts every morning like he is trying to put something down.

encounter.title: Spot Me
encounter.place: Weight room, Pump Iron Gym and Aerobics
encounter.text: Rick Saunders owns Pump Iron, and at six a.m. he is always on the same bench, pushing more weight than a man of thirty-eight should. A dried gardenia hangs from the mirror in his office, brown as a paper bag. When the high school gym next door rattles in the wind, he flinches, every time, like someone dropped a barbell on his heart.
encounter.art: A broad graying man of thirty-eight in a 1980s tank top bench-pressing a heavy bar in an empty gym weight room at dawn, mirrors on every wall, a teenager standing behind the bench spotting the bar with both hands, a small glass office in the background with a dried brown gardenia hanging from its mirror, cold blue dawn light through high windows and one fluorescent tube, medium shot from the side

choices.label: Spot his set and talk while he lifts

success.text: On rep eight, with the bar shaking over his chest, he says it to the ceiling. "There were three of us. Me, Dale, Kenny. We took the ladder. We thought she'd miss the crowning and cry and that would be the funniest thing in the world." He racks the bar and does not get up for a long time. "It rained. Nobody ever asked me what happened. I'd have told them."
success.art: A teenager spotting a barbell over a weeping middle-aged man on a weight bench, morning light through gym windows, chalk dust in the air

failure.text: The bar is heavier than it looks. It sags, he grunts, you both haul it up together, and the moment is gone. "Get out of my gym, kid." As you leave, every mirror in the room steams over and shows a girl in a mint gown standing behind him, hand on his shoulder, very still.
failure.art: Steamed gym mirrors each showing a ghostly prom queen standing behind a man on a weight bench, a teenager backing out of the room

choices.label: Take the dried gardenia off his mirror and ask whose it was

success.text: He snatches for it and stops halfway. "Kenny dared me to take it off her wrist when they carried her inside. I've kept it twenty years so I'd never get to forget." He writes three names on a gym towel with a marker: Dale Hollister, Kenny Albright, Rick Saunders. "Tell her I'm sorry. Tell Delphine first."
success.art: A middle-aged man in a gym office writing three names on a white towel with a marker, a teenager holding a dried brown gardenia corsage, harsh fluorescent light

failure.text: The flower crumbles to brown dust in your fingers. Rick goes white, then red, and bellows you out the door. Behind you, every treadmill in the gym starts up at once, running at full speed with nobody on them, a sound like rain on a roof.
failure.art: A row of empty treadmills running at full speed in a dim gym, brown flower petals scattered on the floor, a teenager fleeing through a glass door

clues.title: The song she never got
clues.hint: KGLM broadcast the 1966 Spring Fling live from the gym. Radio stations never throw out their request cards.

encounter.title: Requests and Dedications
encounter.text: The KGLM record library is a basement of shelves sagging with forty-fives, and a filing cabinet of request cards going back to 1958. Upstairs the overnight show is live. The ON AIR light flickers, and for one second every speaker in the building plays a girl's voice, laughing, saying "Okay, Del, here goes," and then nothing but static.
encounter.art: A radio station basement packed floor to ceiling with shelves of seven-inch vinyl singles, a wooden filing cabinet of pink and white request slips with one drawer pulled open, a teenager flipping through the slips, a red on-air bulb flickering at the top of the stairs, faint gray static shimmering in the air near the speakers, warm bulb light and red glow, medium shot

choices.label: Go through every request card from May 1966

success.text: The card is pink, the pen pressed hard. PLEASE PLAY: Hold Me Till the Morning, The Starlettes. FOR THE QUEEN'S DANCE. Dedicated to D.H. from R.V. Tonight I'm asking her. Paper-clipped to the back, a note from the 1966 DJ: Not played, per the principal. The forty-five is still on the shelf beside it, never opened.
success.art: A pink 1966 radio request card in a teenager's hand with a sealed vinyl single in a paper sleeve, a basement record library around them

failure.text: The drawer jams, then flies open and throws cards into the air like a ticker-tape parade. They fall slowly, too slowly, and every one you catch says the same thing: NOT PLAYED. Somewhere upstairs a record starts, skips and starts again.
failure.art: Hundreds of handwritten request cards floating slowly through a radio station basement, a teenager catching them, each card stamped in red

choices.label: Ask the overnight DJ to put out a call to anyone at the 1966 Spring Fling

success.text: Mix leans into the mic. "If you were at the Spring Fling in '66, the line is open." At 2:14 a.m. an old man calls in: Smokey Lamarr, who spun records that night. "She came to the booth with a card. Wanted one song for the queen's dance. They wouldn't let me play it." His voice cracks. "Card's still in the cabinet, second drawer. I put it back myself."
success.alone: The overnight DJ is out on a smoke break, so you lean into the mic yourself. "If you were at the Spring Fling in '66, the line is open." At 2:14 a.m. an old man calls in: Smokey Lamarr, who spun records that night. "She came to the booth with a card. Wanted one song for the queen's dance. They wouldn't let me play it." His voice cracks. "Card's still in the cabinet, second drawer. I put it back myself."
success.art: A young DJ in headphones at a glowing 1980s radio console taking a call at 2 a.m., a teenager beside him reading a pink request card, the phone line light blinking

failure.text: The phone lines light up, all six at once, and every caller is just rain. Rain and a slow song from very far away. The DJ yanks his headphones off. "Nope. We're playing hair metal until sunrise, and you're going home."
failure.art: A radio console with all six phone line lights blinking at once, a startled DJ pulling off headphones, rain streaking the booth window

signature.title: May I Have This Dance?
signature.place: Glimmer Falls High gym, Spring Fling 1966, in a dream
signature.text: You fall asleep and walk straight into 1966. Paper moons hang from the basketball hoops, a band in white jackets plays the same eight bars over and over, and every couple on the floor is dancing without faces. A girl in a mint gown and a gardenia crown cuts through them toward you, dripping wet. "Have you seen her?" Roz asks. "She said she'd be here."
signature.art: A 1966 high school gym prom at night, paper moons hanging from the basketball hoops, a band in white jackets on a low stage, couples slow-dancing with smooth blank faces, and cutting through them a rain-soaked teenage girl ghost with dark wet curls, freckles, streaked mascara, a mint satin prom gown and a crooked crown of browning gardenias, reaching out a dripping hand toward a teenager in pajamas, soft blue spotlight and silver paper moons, medium wide shot

choices.label: Take her hand and dance while you ask who she means

success.text: Roz dances like a track star, all elbows and enthusiasm, and steps on your feet twice. "Del rides a motorcycle," she tells you, glowing. "She reads Emily Dickinson in the bleachers like it's a dare." The band finally changes songs, and you wake with the smell of gardenias on your hands and the feeling you made a friend.
success.art: A teenager in pajamas slow-dancing with a laughing ghostly prom queen in a mint gown under paper moons, her crown slipping sideways, faceless couples blurring around them

failure.text: The moment you take her hand, she grips hard and does not let go. Around and around, eight bars, eight bars, eight bars. You wake at dawn with your feet aching like you danced all night, your socks wet, and a brown gardenia petal stuck to your cheek.
failure.art: A teenager waking in bed at dawn with wet socks and a brown flower petal on their cheek, faint footprints in water leading across the bedroom carpet

choices.label: Slip between the faceless couples to the fire exit

success.text: You duck under linked arms and past a punch bowl full of rainwater. The fire door bar is ice-cold, and it opens onto your own bedroom ceiling. You jolt awake. On your nightstand someone has left a paper moon, folded small, with one word on it: Del.
success.art: A teenager pushing through a glowing red fire exit door in a dream gym that opens onto their own bedroom, a folded paper moon on a nightstand

failure.text: The exit sign reads 1966. So does the next one, and the next. Every door opens back onto the dance floor, and every time, the faceless couples are closer. When you finally wake, you are standing in your front yard in the rain.
failure.art: A teenager in pajamas standing barefoot in a suburban front yard in the rain at night, a faint glowing exit sign reading 1966 hovering in the dark

signature.title: Rain on the Roof
signature.place: The roof of the Glimmer Falls High gym
signature.text: You wake up soaked, on the flat tar roof of the high school gym, in a storm that did not exist when you went to bed. Your crew is up here too, blinking in their pajamas. The ladder is gone. At the edge of the roof stands Roz, crown streaming, staring down at the parking lot. "This is where they left me," she says. "Let's see who comes for you."
signature.art: Four teenagers in soaked pajamas huddled on the flat tar roof of a high school gym in a lightning storm, rain pouring, the roof ladder gone, a broken drainpipe bracket at the edge, and at the roof's edge a teenage girl ghost in a streaming mint prom gown and a crown of browning gardenias staring down at the dark parking lot, white lightning from above, wide shot

choices.label: Climb down the drainpipe and bring back the ladder

success.text: The pipe is slick and groaning, but you go hand over hand to the bottom, find the ladder rusting behind the dumpster where three boys threw it twenty years ago, and set it against the wall. Your crew climbs down one by one. Roz watches from the edge. "That's how it should have gone," she says, and fades into the rain.
success.art: A drenched teenager bracing an old rusted ladder against a high school gym wall in a storm while friends climb down, a ghostly prom queen watching from the roof edge

failure.text: Halfway down the bracket snaps. You do not fall so much as wake, gasping, on your own lawn, soaked to the bone, with rust on your palms. Your crew wakes on theirs. Nobody wants to talk about the sound the pipe made.
failure.art: A gasping teenager waking on a wet suburban lawn at night with rust stains on their palms, a broken drainpipe bracket clutched in one hand

choices.label: Signal the street below until somebody comes

success.text: Three short, three long, three short. A porch light flicks on across the street, then another. Pearl Washington's station wagon pulls into the lot with Coach Pruitt in the passenger seat and a ladder strapped to the roof. Roz stares at the headlights like she has never seen anything so beautiful. "Somebody came," she whispers.
success.art: A teenager on a stormy gym roof flashing a beam of light toward a suburban street, a station wagon with a ladder on top pulling into the parking lot, porch lights blinking on

failure.text: You flash and flash. The houses stay dark. The rain gets heavier, and Roz turns to you with an awful, gentle pity. "Nobody came for me either." You wake at sunrise, hoarse from shouting, your flashlight dead in your hand.
failure.art: A teenager on a dark gym roof in pouring rain holding up a dying flashlight toward a street of dark houses, a ghostly prom queen beside them with her head bowed

choices.label: Sit beside her at the edge and ask about the note

success.text: Roz pulls a soggy note from her glove. Meet me on the gym roof, look at the stars. "It was her handwriting. Almost. Del dots her i's with circles because I told her it was cute." She laughs and it turns into a sob. "I knew on the third rung. I came up anyway, just in case." The rain softens to a drizzle around you both.
success.art: A teenager and a ghostly prom queen sitting side by side on a rainy gym roof edge, the ghost holding up a soggy forged note, the storm softening around them

failure.text: "You want to know about the note?" Roz turns, and lightning shows you the whole night at once: the laughing boys, the missing ladder, the pipe. You wake with your hands clenched so hard your nails have left little moons in your palms.
failure.art: A lightning flash revealing ghostly images of three laughing teenage boys carrying a ladder away from a gym wall, a terrified teen in the foreground

signature.title: Look Up
signature.place: Glimmer Falls High gym, Halloween Hop rehearsal, after dark
signature.text: The student council is rehearsing the Halloween Hop crowning, and Chip Merriweather is standing on the stage in a cardboard crown beside Tasha Greene, who is practicing her surprised face. You glance up. In the rafters above the stage hangs a galvanized bucket on a fraying rope, dripping, and next to it, sitting on the catwalk with her mint gown hanging down like a curtain, is Roz. "Every year somebody thinks it's funny," she says. "And every year nobody looks up."
signature.art: A high school gym stage after dark, a preppy 17-year-old boy with side-parted chestnut hair and a navy blazer and a girl in a sweater both wearing cardboard crowns rehearsing a coronation, high above them in the rafters a dripping galvanized bucket hanging on a fraying rope, and seated on the catwalk beside it a teenage girl ghost in a mint prom gown and gardenia crown with her skirt hanging down, a teenager below looking up, stage work lights and dark rafters, low angle shot from the floor

choices.label: Climb the catwalk ladder and grab the bucket before it drops

success.text: You shinny up the ladder and get both hands on the rope just as the last strand gives. The bucket is heavier than it looks. Inside is a quart of lime gelatin and a card in a jock's blocky print: For Our Queen. Roz looks at it for a long time. "Lime," she says. "Mine was rain."
success.art: A teenager on a high gym catwalk gripping a fraying rope and a heavy galvanized bucket of green gelatin, a ghostly prom queen in a mint gown seated beside them, a student rehearsal on the stage far below

failure.text: You are halfway up when the rope lets go. The bucket swings down in a perfect arc and empties over you instead of the stage: ice-cold rainwater full of brown gardenia petals. The whole gym laughs, and for one horrible second the laughter has an echo to it, like a gym full of people from 1966.
failure.art: A teenager clinging to a gym ladder drenched by a swinging bucket of rainwater and brown flower petals, students on the stage below laughing, faint ghostly 1966 dancers echoing among them

choices.label: Shout for everyone to get off the stage, right now

success.text: "Everybody off! Fire drill! Free pizza!" Chip backs you up in his best class-president voice, and the stage empties in ten seconds flat. The bucket drops onto the crowning spot with a crash and a green splash. Up in the rafters, Roz claps slowly, and then, surprising everyone including herself, she laughs.
success.art: Students scrambling off a high school stage as a galvanized bucket crashes down and splashes green gelatin across the boards, a preppy teen in a cardboard crown waving everyone clear, a ghostly prom queen laughing in the rafters

failure.text: Everybody thinks you're doing a bit. Tasha even curtsies. You end up sprinting onstage to shove her clear yourself, and the bucket clangs down over your head like a cartoon bell. You stand there dripping and wearing it while the Hop committee gives you a standing ovation.
failure.art: A dripping teenager standing on a high school stage with a galvanized bucket upside down over their head, green gelatin oozing down their shoulders, a student committee applauding from folding chairs

choices.label: Call up to Roz and ask who hung the bucket

success.text: "Look at the knot," Roz says. It's a lineman's hitch, the same knot three boys used on a ladder in 1966. You follow her finger down to the bleachers, where two junior varsity guys are trying very hard to look innocent. One word from you and the whole student council turns to stare at them. For once, the people who rigged the joke are the ones everybody is looking at.
success.art: A ghostly prom queen on a gym catwalk pointing down at two guilty-looking teenage boys in varsity jackets on the bleachers, a student council turning to stare at them, a teenager at the foot of the ladder

failure.text: Roz leans over the catwalk until her crown nearly falls. "You want to know who?" The gym lights stutter, and every bleacher seat in the building slams up and down like thunderous applause. When it stops, the rehearsal has fled, the bucket is gone, and you are alone with a puddle shaped like a crown.
failure.art: A dim high school gym with bleacher seats flapping wildly in the flickering lights, a furious ghostly prom queen leaning from the catwalk, a lone teenager beside a puddle shaped like a crown

signature.title: Say Her Name Three Times
signature.place: A slumber party at the Okafor house, midnight
signature.text: Nkechi Okafor's slumber party has reached the part of the night where somebody lights a candle and lines everyone up in front of the bathroom mirror. "Say Spring Queen three times," Nkechi whispers, "and she crowns you." Five sleepy kids and you giggle through it. On the third time the giggling stops, because in the mirror everyone is wearing a 1966 gown or a white dinner jacket, and standing behind them, dripping, is Roz. She does not look flattered. "A game," she says. "I'm a game now."
signature.art: A candlelit pink-tiled bathroom at a slumber party at midnight, five kids in pajamas crowded in front of the mirror holding a candle, and in the mirror their reflections wearing 1966 prom gowns and white dinner jackets, with a dripping teenage girl ghost in a mint gown and a crown of browning gardenias standing behind them in the glass, unsmiling, warm candle flame and cold blue mirror light, medium shot from behind the kids

choices.label: Say her real name and tell everyone what actually happened

success.text: "Her name is Rosalind Vance," you say, "and she wasn't a ghost story. She was a track star who was going to ask a girl to dance." The candle steadies. In the mirror the gowns fade back to pajamas, and Roz's reflection looks at each kid in turn, like she is memorizing who listened. "That's so much sadder," Nkechi whispers, and nobody ever plays the game again.
success.art: Kids in pajamas sitting quietly on a bathroom floor around a steady candle, listening to a teenager speak, in the mirror a ghostly prom queen gazing gently at each of them, her gardenia crown glowing softly

failure.text: You start to explain, but it comes out the way the town always told it: a silly girl, a roof, a storm. Roz's reflection goes rigid. The mirror fogs, and a fingertip traces the word ACCIDENT in the steam and underlines it twice. The candle blows out, and six kids scream in perfect harmony.
failure.art: A fogged bathroom mirror with a ghostly fingertip tracing streaks through the steam, a candle smoking as it gutters out, kids in pajamas screaming and clutching each other in the dark

choices.label: Throw a bath towel over the mirror and get everyone out

success.text: Towel over the glass, candle in the sink, kids out the door in a stampede of sleeping bags. You hold the door shut while the faucet runs by itself for a full minute. Then it stops, and from under the door creeps one small, polite puddle and a single gardenia petal.
success.art: A teenager holding a bathroom door shut in a dark hallway while kids in pajamas flee dragging sleeping bags, a small puddle and a single white gardenia petal creeping out from under the door

failure.text: The towel slides off as if someone tugged it. Every reflection turns to look at you, and then the hall mirror, the compact in Nkechi's purse and the back of a spoon in the kitchen all show the same wet girl, all night, wherever you look.
failure.art: A frightened teenager in a dark kitchen staring at the back of a shiny spoon, the reflection showing a dripping ghostly prom queen in a gardenia crown, a towel slipping off a hallway mirror behind them

choices.label: Grab the dress-up tiara and crown Roz instead

success.text: You hold a dime-store tiara up to the mirror over Roz's reflection and announce her in your best pageant voice: "Your Spring Queen, Rosalind Vance!" The slumber party catches on and hums a wobbly processional. Roz's reflection puts a hand over her mouth. "Nobody announced me," she says. "They just read my name and played the song."
success.art: A teenager holding a sparkly dime-store tiara up to a bathroom mirror where it rests on a ghostly prom queen's head, kids in pajamas humming a procession behind them, the ghost covering her mouth with delight

failure.text: The tiara touches the glass and the mirror crowns you back. You spend the rest of the night unable to take off a crown of wet, wilted gardenias that only you can feel, and every time you laugh, you taste rain.
failure.art: A teenager in pajamas lying awake in a sleeping bag wearing a crown of wet wilted gardenias, raindrops trickling down their forehead, sleeping kids around them in a dark living room

signature.title: Need a Lift?
signature.place: Quarry Road in the rain, 11 p.m.
signature.text: The late activity bus home from the Pine Ridge away game is crawling down Quarry Road through a storm that came out of a clear sky. In the headlights a girl in a mint gown stands on the shoulder with her shoes in her hand and her crown streaming, and Mrs. Dombrowski stops, because Mrs. Dombrowski always stops. The girl climbs on, drips down the aisle and sits beside you. "Is this the bus to the gym?" Roz asks. "I'm so late. She's waiting." You know this story from every sleepover of your life, and it never ends with the girl getting where she's going.
signature.art: The inside of a yellow school bus at night crawling down a rainy country road, headlights cutting through the downpour beyond the windshield, an older woman bus driver at the wheel, a teenager on a green vinyl seat beside a soaked teenage girl ghost in a mint prom gown holding her shoes in her lap, her crown of gardenias dripping, rain streaming down the windows, dim dome light and green dashboard glow, medium shot down the aisle

choices.label: Give her your jacket and keep her talking all the way to the gym

success.text: She pulls your jacket on over her gown and talks the whole way: relay splits, a girl who fixes her own motorcycle, a song she has been saving. At the school gates the seat beside you is suddenly vacant and warm. Your jacket is folded on it, bone dry and smelling of gardenias, and in the pocket is a ticket stub from the 1966 Spring Fling.
success.art: A teenager on a school bus seat holding up an old ticket stub, a neatly folded jacket on the warm vinyl seat beside them, a single gardenia petal resting on it, rain-streaked windows glowing with school gate lights

failure.text: She takes the jacket and goes quiet, staring out at the rain. At the school gates she is gone, and so is your jacket. In the morning you find it hanging off the gym's drainpipe two stories up, soaked through, flapping in the wind like a flag.
failure.art: A soaked teenage jacket snagged on a drainpipe high on a brick high school gym wall at dawn, flapping in the wind, a tired teenager staring up at it from the wet parking lot

choices.label: Watch her in the bus driver's big mirror instead of looking right at her

success.text: In the mirror, the seat beside you holds a seventeen-year-old in a wet gown, shivering, chewing her thumbnail, more nervous than scary. She is rehearsing under her breath: Del, will you dance with me. Del, will you. When you look back at the seat itself, there is only a puddle, and you understand you just heard a girl practice asking.
success.art: The wide rearview mirror of a school bus reflecting a nervous teenage girl in a wet mint gown biting her lip, the actual bus seat beside a teenager holding a small puddle of rainwater

failure.text: In the mirror the whole bus is full of her, a girl in a mint gown in every seat, every one of them turning slowly to look at you. Mrs. Dombrowski slams the brakes, and the bus slides gently into a ditch full of rainwater, where it sits until the tow truck comes at dawn.
failure.art: A bus driver's rearview mirror showing ghostly prom queens in mint gowns filling every seat and turning to stare, a yellow school bus tilted in a flooded roadside ditch in the rain

choices.label: Tell Mrs. Dombrowski to floor it and beat the storm to the gym

success.text: You call the curves from the front step like a rally navigator, and Mrs. Dombrowski takes Quarry Road like a getaway driver. The bus skids into the school lot at 11:59 with every passenger whooping. Roz is on her feet before the doors fold open. "On time," she breathes. "I was never on time for anything." She runs into the rain toward the gym, laughing.
success.art: A yellow school bus skidding into a rainy high school parking lot in a spray of water, whooping teenagers at the windows, a ghostly prom queen in a mint gown running laughing toward glowing gym doors

failure.text: The bus fishtails on the wet curve and every window fogs at once with the same small handprint. When the glass clears, you are parked at the gym in total silence, the seat beside you wet, the dashboard clock stopped at 11:59, and nobody on the bus can remember the last ten minutes.
failure.art: The fogged windows of a school bus at night each marked with the same small handprint, a dashboard clock stopped at 11:59, dazed teenagers sitting silent in their seats outside a dark high school gym

signature.title: Couples Only
signature.text: Every radio on Crystal Street switches on at once and plays the same slow song, skipping on the same scratch. Out of every front door come couples in their pajamas and curlers, sound asleep, waltzing down the driveways toward the high school. The Szymanskis. The newlyweds on the corner. Your own parents, eyes closed, dancing better than you have ever seen them dance. Roz sits on the Heartstone like a throne, conducting.
signature.art: A suburban cul-de-sac at two in the morning, sleepwalking couples in pajamas and hair curlers waltzing with closed eyes down their driveways toward the street, radios glowing in every window, a middle-aged couple dancing gracefully in the foreground, and in the center of the roundabout a teenage girl ghost in a mint prom gown and a gardenia crown sitting on a huge purple crystal rock conducting with both hands, a teenager in pajamas on a lawn, blue moonlight and warm window light, wide shot

choices.label: Cut in on Roz herself and lead her off the Heartstone

success.text: You bow, you offer your hand, you dip her so dramatically that Mrs. Szymanski's curlers fall out. Roz shrieks with laughter despite herself. The song skips past its scratch for the first time, the couples stumble awake in the street, and Roz says, "Not bad. Not her, but not bad."
success.art: A teenager dramatically dipping a laughing ghostly prom queen in front of a glowing purple geode, waking couples in pajamas blinking around them in the street

failure.text: Roz takes your hand and you are a couple now, too. You waltz down Crystal Street with your eyes closed, unable to stop, all the way to the gym doors. You wake there at dawn, slumped against them, a gardenia pinned to your pajama shirt.
failure.art: A teenager asleep slumped against high school gym doors at dawn, a wilted gardenia corsage pinned to their pajama shirt, dew on the steps

choices.label: Run house to house yanking radio plugs

success.text: Kitchen radio, clock radio, a boombox in a bathroom. Your crew splits up and calls each house over channel nine. When the last plug comes out, the street goes silent, and forty couples wake up in the road at once, holding hands, deeply confused, some of them a little bit charmed.
success.art: Teenagers sprinting between suburban houses yanking radio plugs from walls, confused couples in bathrobes waking up holding hands in the middle of the street

failure.text: You unplug a radio and it keeps playing. You pull out its batteries and it keeps playing. Behind you, the couples pick up the pace, and a sleepwalking Mr. Szymanski tangoes you into a hedge.
failure.art: An unplugged clock radio still glowing and playing on a kitchen counter, a teenager tangled in a hedge while a sleepwalking man in a robe dances away

choices.label: Stand in front of your parents and wake them by name

success.text: You say their names, then the embarrassing nicknames they use when they think you cannot hear. Your mom opens her eyes mid-twirl and laughs. "We used to dance like this before you were born." Roz goes very quiet on the Heartstone, watching them hold on to each other on purpose.
success.art: A teenager in pajamas facing their sleepwalking parents in the street, the parents opening their eyes mid-dance and laughing, a ghostly prom queen watching wistfully from a glowing geode

failure.text: They dance around you like you are a lamppost. Your dad hums the scratched song in your mother's ear, and neither of them hears you at all. You stand alone in the middle of Crystal Street until the radios click off at dawn.
failure.art: A lonely teenager standing in the middle of a dim suburban street while sleepwalking couples dance around them as if they were invisible, radios glowing in windows

signature.title: Special Delivery
signature.place: Your front porch on Crystal Street, midnight
signature.text: At midnight the doorbell rings once, politely. Nobody is on the porch, only a clear plastic florist's box tied with mint ribbon and beaded with rainwater, though the sky is full of stars. Inside is a wrist corsage of three gardenias, browning at the edges, and a tiny card in looping cursive: Save the last dance. R. A line of wet footprints leads off the porch toward the high school, and the whole yard smells like a storm that happened twenty years ago.
signature.art: A suburban front porch at midnight under a clear starry sky, a clear plastic florist box tied with mint ribbon and beaded with rainwater on the welcome mat, a wrist corsage of three browning gardenias inside, a line of wet footprints leading down the porch steps and along the sidewalk toward a distant high school gym, a teenager in pajamas in the open doorway, yellow porch light and starlight, medium wide shot

choices.label: Slip the corsage on your wrist and follow the wet footprints

success.text: The footprints lead you down Crystal Street, around the Heartstone and up to the gym doors, where they stop toes together, like someone waiting to be let in. The corsage on your wrist turns warm. Behind you a girl's voice says, "Thanks for walking me. Nobody ever walks me," and when you turn there is only a puddle shaped like a high-heeled shoe.
success.art: A teenager in socks standing at the doors of a high school gym at night, a gardenia corsage glowing on one wrist, a puddle shaped like a high-heeled shoe on the step, wet footprints ending toe to toe

failure.text: The footprints lead you in circles around the Heartstone, faster and faster, until you are jogging in your socks and the corsage is cinched tight as a blood-pressure cuff. You wake on the roundabout lawn at three in the morning with wet feet and a gardenia petal in each fist.
failure.art: A teenager in wet socks sprawled on a moonlit roundabout lawn beside a giant purple geode, fists full of gardenia petals, a looping trail of wet footprints circling the grass

choices.label: Put it in the fridge like a real corsage and keep it safe for whoever it's for

success.text: You tuck the box in the vegetable crisper the way your aunt kept her prom flowers and stick a note on it for the family: DO NOT EAT. By morning the gardenias are snow white and fresh, and the little card has changed. Now it reads: For Del. Please get it to her. The corsage was never for you. You were just the one who answered the door.
success.art: A refrigerator vegetable crisper glowing in a dark kitchen, a florist box holding snow white gardenias tied with mint ribbon, a small handwritten card tucked in the bow, a teenager in pajamas smiling down at it

failure.text: The fridge hums, shudders and fills with rain. In the morning every shelf is a puddle, the milk carton is floating, and the corsage has sprouted a tangle of brown stems that wraps the eggs like a vine. Your mom takes one look, closes the fridge and walks away.
failure.art: An open refrigerator flooded with rainwater at dawn, a milk carton floating on a shelf, brown gardenia stems curling around an egg carton, a parent in a bathrobe squinting at it in disbelief

choices.label: Call the after-hours number printed on the florist's box

success.text: It rings and rings, and then a cheerful woman picks up through a crackle of 1966 static. "Petal and Stem, after-hours orders! Oh, the Vance corsage. Paid in full, to be delivered to the gym for Miss Hart, Spring Fling night. Was there a problem, hon?" You tell her it never got there. There is a long pause, and then she says softly, "Oh, that poor girl," and the dial tone sounds like rain.
success.art: A teenager on a yellow kitchen wall phone at midnight, a florist box open on the counter, a faint shimmering vision of a 1960s flower shop with buckets of gardenias glowing in the air behind them

failure.text: A busy signal. Then the receiver goes cold and wet in your hand, and the busy signal turns into a slow-dance song, the same eight bars over and over. You hang up. The phone rings back every fifteen minutes until dawn, and every time you lift it, the band is still playing.
failure.art: A yellow kitchen wall phone dripping with rainwater at three in the morning, a tired teenager in pajamas staring at the ringing receiver, gardenia petals drifting across the linoleum

signature.title: Rain Check
signature.place: Main Street at dusk, walking home past the library
signature.text: It is a clear, warm evening on Main Street, and it is raining on you. Only you. A stubborn little storm cloud the size of a beach umbrella followed you out of the pharmacy, and it drizzles on your head while people stop to stare: Mr. Park sweeping outside his dry cleaners, two kids on BMX bikes, a Gazette reporter raising a camera. Inside the cloud, something hums a slow song. Whoever Roz is waiting for, she has decided you are going to help her find them.
signature.art: A small-town main street at a warm golden dusk, a teenager walking down the sidewalk under a tiny gray storm cloud the size of a beach umbrella raining only on them, puddles at their feet, a Korean American shopkeeper with a broom staring from the dry cleaner's door, two kids on bikes pointing, a reporter raising a camera, library steps ahead, golden sunlight on dry pavement everywhere else, wide shot

choices.label: Walk your little storm up the library steps to Ms. Hart

success.text: You drip across the marble lobby and Ms. Hart looks up from the returns cart. She does not ask. She steps out from behind the desk and stands under your cloud with you, rain spotting her cardigan, eyes closed. "Gardenias," she says. "She hated umbrellas. Said they were for people who weren't sure." For one minute the drizzle is warm as bathwater, and then the cloud thins to blue.
success.art: A librarian in a cardigan standing with her eyes closed beside a teenager under a small indoor rain cloud in a marble library lobby, warm drizzle falling, gardenia petals scattered on the floor

failure.text: You make it up the steps, but the cloud gets nervous at the door and pours. Water sheets across the lobby, the microfiche reader sparks, and you spend the evening helping Ms. Hart lay the newspaper archive out to dry on every table. She keeps glancing at the ceiling like she is listening for something she missed.
failure.art: A flooded library lobby with old newspapers spread to dry across every table, a teenager with a mop, a librarian in a cardigan gazing up at a dripping ceiling

choices.label: Swing around a lamppost and sing in the rain like a big movie-musical number

success.text: You hook one arm around a lamppost and belt the only rain song you know, splashing in the gutter, and the BMX kids join in. Mr. Park taps his broom in time. The little cloud swirls like a dancing skirt, the drizzle turns to glitter in the streetlight, and somewhere inside it a girl laughs, delighted, like she has never been the audience before.
success.art: A teenager swinging around a lamppost on a twilight main street, splashing in the gutter, two BMX kids singing along, a small storm cloud overhead swirling like a skirt and sparkling with glitter

failure.text: Your voice cracks on the first high note, your sneaker slips, and you sit down hard in a puddle in front of half of Main Street. The Gazette reporter takes another photo. The cloud thunders once, embarrassed for both of you, and follows you home, soaking you to the skin.
failure.art: A soaked teenager sitting in a gutter puddle on a twilight main street, a small grumbling thundercloud overhead, a reporter snapping a camera, shopkeepers wincing from their doorsteps

choices.label: Cut through backyards and shortcuts to lose the cloud before the whole town sees

success.text: Through the Okafors' side gate, under a carport, across the high school parking lot at a sprint. The cloud snags on the gym's drainpipe, the very one, and stays there, raining softly on that single corner of the roof. You watch from the shadows as it drizzles in a slow circle, like someone pacing.
success.art: A small gray rain cloud snagged on the drainpipe of a high school gym at dusk, raining in a slow circle on one corner of the roof, a teenager watching from the shadow of the bleachers

failure.text: The cloud keeps up with every shortcut, and by the time you reach Crystal Street it is the size of a garage and has brought thunder. Half the street watches from their lawns as you sprint home under a private downpour, and your little neighbor asks if you are cursed.
failure.art: A teenager sprinting down a suburban cul-de-sac at dusk under a huge private thundercloud, neighbors watching from their lawns, a little kid on a tricycle pointing

signature.title: Pass It On
signature.place: Glimmer Falls High gym, Halloween Hop decorating night, October 30
signature.text: The Hop committee is hanging orange streamers when the gym clock spins backward and the storm comes in through the ceiling. The streamers turn into paper moons, the bleachers fill with faceless boys in 1966 letterman jackets, and a folded sheet of pink stationery starts traveling hand to hand up the rows, every echo laughing as he reads it. You know what it is. It is Roz's letter, the one about asking Del to dance, and it is two rows from the three boys waiting at the top. On the stage, Roz watches it climb, white-knuckled, as if this time someone might stop it.
signature.art: A high school gym at night in a sudden indoor rainstorm, orange paper streamers turning into silver paper moons, bleachers full of boys in 1960s letterman jackets with smooth blank faces passing a folded sheet of pink stationery hand to hand up the rows, three boys waiting at the top row, a teenager climbing the bleachers in a crouch, and on the stage a rain-soaked girl ghost in a mint gown and gardenia crown gripping her skirt, white lightning flashes, wide shot

choices.label: Slip up the bleachers and snatch the letter before it reaches the top row

success.text: You go up the rows in a crouch, under elbows, around knees, and pluck the pink letter out of an echo's hand one row from the top. The laughter stops like a needle lifted off a record. On the stage, Roz breathes out for what looks like the first time in twenty years. You tuck the letter, still folded, safe inside your jacket.
success.art: A teenager crouched on rainy gym bleachers clutching a folded pink letter, faceless boys in letterman jackets frozen mid-laugh around them, a ghostly prom queen on the stage sighing with relief

failure.text: An echo holds the letter high, out of reach, and passes it over your head. It lands in the hands of the three at the top, who read it aloud in voices like a broken radio. The whole gym of echoes laughs, and the storm comes down so hard the Hop streamers wash off the walls.
failure.art: Three faceless boys in 1960s letterman jackets on the top row of gym bleachers holding a pink letter high, rain pouring from the rafters, streamers washing off the walls, a teenager reaching up below

choices.label: Take the letter and read it to the whole gym yourself, the way it deserved to be heard

success.text: You unfold it and read every word into the Hop committee's microphone: a girl planning to cross a dance floor in front of everyone and ask another girl to dance, scared and sure and funny about it. The echoes stop laughing. One by one they fade. The real Hop committee stands in the rain with their mouths open, and then Tasha from student council starts clapping, and everyone does. Roz puts both hands over her face.
success.art: A teenager reading a pink letter into a microphone in a rainy gym, a decorating committee applauding, ghostly boys in letterman jackets fading on the bleachers, a prom queen in a gardenia crown covering her face on the stage

failure.text: Your voice wobbles, and the echoes laugh over the first line, louder with every sentence, until you cannot hear yourself. You stop. The storm stops with you, the way a held breath stops, and Roz turns away on the stage. The letter goes soggy and blank in your hands.
failure.art: A teenager holding a soggy sheet of pink stationery in a stormy gym, faceless boys laughing on the bleachers, a prom queen in a mint gown turning away on the stage

choices.label: Climb to the top row and stare down the three boys waiting for the letter

success.text: You plant yourself in front of them: three faceless jackets and three smirks. "It's not yours," you say. "It never was." They look at each other. Without a crowd laughing along, they are just three nervous boys in borrowed jackets, and they fade like breath on cold glass. The letter drifts down through the rain into Roz's hands.
success.art: A teenager standing tall on the top row of gym bleachers facing three fading boys in letterman jackets, a pink letter drifting down through the rain toward a prom queen on the stage

failure.text: The three of them stand up together, much taller than boys should be, and the bleachers rattle like thunder under your feet. You lose your footing and slide down ten rows on your back. When you look up the letter is gone, and the 1966 laughter goes on echoing in the rafters until dawn.
failure.art: A teenager sliding down rain-slick gym bleachers on their back, three towering faceless boys in letterman jackets standing on the top row, lightning flashing through the high gym rafters

finale.title: The Queen's Dance
finale.place: Glimmer Falls High gym, Halloween night, and also May 1966
finale.text: On Halloween night the gym doors open onto 1966. The storm is inside now, rain falling from the rafters onto paper moons, and every couple in Glimmer Falls is frozen mid-sway on the floor. Roz stands on the stage in her gardenia crown, lightning in her hair, the band behind her playing the same eight bars forever. "They took my dance," she says. "So nobody leaves the floor. Not tonight. Not ever."
finale.art: A high school gym on Halloween night turned into a 1966 prom, rain falling from the rafters through paper moons, hundreds of couples frozen mid-sway on the wet floor, a band in white jackets behind the stage, and on the stage a furious teenage girl ghost with dark wet curls, a crooked crown of browning gardenias, a mint satin gown and lightning crackling in her hair, four teenagers in homemade Halloween costumes at the open doors, white lightning and blue rain light, wide shot

choices.label: Force open every door and drag the couples out into the night

success.text: You jam the doors with folding chairs and haul frozen couples out two at a time into the cold October air, where they wake gasping. When the last pair is out, the gym storm collapses into a puddle on the floorboards, and Roz is just gone, like a song cut off before the end.
success.art: Teens hauling frozen couples out of a stormy gym into cold October night air, folding chairs jammed in the doors, a ghostly prom queen fading in the rain behind them

failure.text: The doors slam back on you, and the couple you were pulling drifts out of your hands into the dance. Your feet start to move on their own. One, two, three. One, two, three. The band plays the eight bars again.
failure.art: A teen's feet sliding into a waltz step against their will on a rain-slick gym floor, frozen couples closing in, gym doors slamming shut

choices.label: Crown a new Spring Queen and start the coronation without her

success.text: You grab the mic, announce a write-in winner and crown the biggest, gruffest dad in the room with a paper moon. The frozen couples cheer on reflex. Roz stares, outraged that anyone would steal her moment, and the spell that holds the floor snaps like a rubber band. She vanishes in a crack of thunder, still yelling.
success.art: A teen at a microphone crowning a startled burly dad in pajamas with a paper moon tiara, couples cheering, a furious prom queen ghost cracking into thunder

failure.text: "Oh, you want a coronation?" Roz lifts the crown off her own head and sets it on yours. It is soaking wet and heavy as a stone, and you understand you will be standing in this gym for a very long time.
failure.art: A ghostly prom queen placing a dripping gardenia crown on a horrified teenager's head on a rainy gym stage

choices.label: Play the song she requested in 1966 and open the doors for Delphine

success.text: You hold up the photo they never printed and the three names Rick finally said out loud, and then you drop the needle on the forty-five nobody ever opened. Hold Me Till the Morning, by the Starlettes. The rain stops in midair. The gym doors swing open and Delphine Hart walks in, leather jacket, cardigan, Roz's ring on her finger, crying already. "I came," she says. "I'm late. I'm so sorry I'm late." Roz drops the lightning.
success.art: A middle-aged woman in a leather jacket over a cardigan walking into a rain-frozen 1966 prom gym, raindrops hanging in midair, a prom queen ghost on stage dropping her lightning, a teen lowering a record needle onto a turntable

failure.text: The needle skips. The song warps into a moan, and the storm swallows the doorway. You have the truth in your hands, the photo, the names and the song, but the gym is too loud with twenty years of thunder for Roz to hear it.
failure.art: A record needle skipping on a warped spinning single, a storm swallowing the gym doorway, a teen holding up a photograph that a raging prom queen ghost cannot see

choices.label: Look up, like you learned to the first week, and find what she has rigged in the rafters

success.text: Since the first nights of the week you have known what Roz knows: every year, nobody looks up. You do. High in the rafters over the frozen couples hangs a galvanized bucket full of thunder on a fraying rope. You climb, swing it wide, and tip it out over the bare stage in one huge crash of rain. The storm runs out with it. The couples blink awake mid-sway, the band finally lands on a new chord, and Roz, soaked and startled, laughs out loud at the oldest prank in the book turned around.
success.art: A teenager on a high gym catwalk tipping a galvanized bucket of storm water onto a bare stage, frozen prom couples waking below under paper moons, a soaked prom queen in a gardenia crown laughing

failure.text: You spot the bucket in the rafters, but the catwalk ladder is slick and you miss the rope by an inch. The bucket swings down and empties over you instead, cold rain and brown gardenia petals, and the frozen floor chuckles in an echo from 1966. You are soaked, but the other ways out are still open.
failure.art: A drenched teenager clinging to a catwalk ladder in a stormy gym, a swinging galvanized bucket spilling rain and brown gardenia petals over them, frozen couples below under paper moons

choices.label: Walk into her storm the way you did all week and stop the band yourself

success.text: All week you stood in Roz's rain, on a roof, in a mirror, on Main Street, and it never washed you away. You walk straight through the storm, past the frozen couples and the lightning, climb onto the stage and stand in front of the band in white jackets with both hands up like a crossing guard. "That's the last song," you say. The band stops mid-bar. In the silence the couples stagger free, and Roz stares at you through the rain like someone who has finally been told no by a person who cares what happens to her.
success.art: A teenager standing on a gym stage with both hands raised in front of a band in white jackets, rain falling from the rafters onto paper moons, couples waking on the dance floor, a prom queen staring

failure.text: The storm shoves back. Wind howls through the gym and drives you to one knee halfway across the floor, rain stinging your face, and the band plays louder to drown you out. You are still standing, barely, and there is a way through tonight, just not this one.
failure.art: A teenager down on one knee on a gym dance floor in an indoor storm, wind and rain whipping paper moons, a band in white jackets playing on behind a prom queen crowned with lightning

choices.label: Say her love out loud again, like the night before Halloween, and open the doors for Delphine

success.text: The night before Halloween you said out loud what three boys laughed at in 1966. Tonight you say it into the band's microphone, for the whole frozen floor: Roz Vance was going to cross this gym and ask Delphine Hart to dance. You drop the needle on the forty-five nobody ever opened, the doors swing wide, and Delphine walks in out of the dark in her leather jacket with Roz's ring on her finger. The rain stops in midair. Roz looks at you once, a thank-you, and steps down off the stage to cross the floor exactly the way she planned.
success.art: A librarian in a leather jacket and cardigan stepping through open gym doors, raindrops frozen in midair, a prom queen in a mint gown and gardenia crown descending the stage steps toward her, a teenager by a record player smiling

failure.text: You start to tell the gym the truth, but the thunder rolls over every word, and the doors stick on twenty years of swollen wood. Delphine is out there; you can hear her motorcycle idling in the lot. Roz hears it too, and the storm wavers, but it does not break yet.
failure.art: A teenager at a microphone in a stormy gym shouting over thunder, rain-swollen double doors stuck half open, motorcycle headlights glowing in the parking lot beyond, a prom queen on the stage turning toward the light

best.title: Hold Me Till the Morning
best.text: Roz steps down off the stage and crosses the whole floor in front of everyone, exactly the way she planned it in 1966, and asks Delphine Hart to dance. The frozen couples wake up and make room. For three minutes and ten seconds two girls who were never allowed to are the only thing anyone in Glimmer Falls is looking at, and Roz steps on Delphine's feet twice, and they laugh so hard they have to stop. When the song ends, Roz kisses the ring on Delphine's hand, puts her gardenia crown on Delphine's head and goes up through the rafters like a firework, laughing. The rain is gone. The stars are out. That spring the yearbook prints the milkshake photo on its first page, and Ms. Hart chaperones a prom where anyone can ask anyone, and she dances every single song.
best.art: A teenage girl ghost in a mint prom gown and a crown of gardenias slow-dancing with a freckled 38-year-old woman with gray-streaked chestnut hair, tortoiseshell glasses and an oxblood cardigan in the middle of a high school gym under paper moons, both laughing, couples in pajamas and Halloween costumes standing in a circle around them, starlight pouring through an open roof, gardenia petals falling, silver light, wide shot

good.title: The Floor Is Closed
good.text: The couples of Glimmer Falls wake up in the gym parking lot at dawn holding hands, with no idea why their feet hurt. The storm is over. Roz is gone, or at least quiet. You never find out what song she was waiting for. Some nights, driving past the high school, you could swear there is someone on the roof, looking at the stars, still waiting for a ladder.
good.art: Confused couples in pajamas and curlers waking up in a high school parking lot at dawn still holding hands, rubbing their eyes and looking at their bare feet, puddles on the asphalt, and on the gym roof against the pink sunrise the small silhouette of a girl in a long gown looking up at the fading stars, wide shot

bittersweet.title: A Gardenia in the Rain
bittersweet.text: You get the town off the dance floor, but not everyone at once. For weeks a few couples on Crystal Street keep sleepwalking into the road at two a.m., swaying to music only they can hear. Ms. Hart quietly stops wearing the ring and starts wearing it again. Every May, a gardenia appears on the gym roof, and nobody ever admits to putting it there.
bittersweet.art: A single white gardenia lying on the wet tar roof of a high school gym at dawn, beads of rain on its petals, and far below on a suburban street a sleepwalking couple in pajamas swaying together in the road, pale pink morning light, close foreground with a wide background

bad.title: Forever 1966
bad.text: On November first your friends find you asleep on the gym floor, and you do not wake up for them. Behind your eyelids it is always May 1966, the band always playing the same eight bars, and you are dancing with a girl in a dripping crown who never stops looking at the door. Your crew plays every slow song ever recorded at your bedside, trying to find the one that ends it.
bad.art: A teenager asleep on a narrow cot in a dim bedroom, three worried friends around the bed with a portable record player and stacks of seven-inch singles, and floating above them a faint pale image of the same teenager slow-dancing with a girl ghost in a mint prom gown in an empty gym under paper moons, warm lamp light and silver glow, medium wide shot
